name: Minoxidil for chest hair

lead: Forum users in chest-hair discussions apply topical minoxidil, a scalp hair-loss treatment, to the chest hoping for denser or longer hair. It is an off-label use.

Minoxidil is a prodrug converted by the enzyme SULT1A1 to minoxidil sulfate, which opens potassium channels. Its effect on hair is not fully understood; proposed actions include increased blood flow, growth-factor stimulation and a longer follicle growth phase. A registered phase 4 trial of 3% minoxidil lotion for chest hair enhancement (NCT02283645, 64 participants, started 2015) exists, but its status is listed as unknown and no results were found.

paras: Users apply the lotion or foam to the chest daily as part of a routine, alongside not shaving, and look for changes over months. Reference sources report hair loss resumes after stopping when used for scalp loss.

Topical minoxidil can cause itching, irritation, dandruff, temporary shedding and unwanted hair growth on other body areas. Oral minoxidil carries cardiovascular effects and is prescription-only in the US. It is approved for scalp pattern hair loss, not chest hair.

angle.text: Chest-hair-maxxing forums apply topical minoxidil, approved for scalp hair loss, to the chest hoping to stimulate follicles for denser, longer hair. One registered trial of 3% lotion for chest hair exists, with no published results found.

lead: Minoxidil for chest hair is the off-label use of topical minoxidil, a drug approved for pattern hair loss on the scalp, on the chest to make hair look thicker or denser. It is discussed in appearance communities as part of "chest hair maxxing", where a fuller chest is treated as part of a more masculine look.[1]

Chest hair is terminal hair that develops from puberty onward as androgens rise, and its amount, pattern and thickness are mainly genetic; Wikipedia notes that men range from very hairy to having none, all described as normal.[2] Minoxidil is also used off-label to encourage beard and facial hair, including in transgender men, according to Wikipedia, which cites studies without reporting their results.

A phase 4 trial, "Efficacy and Safety of 3% Minoxidil Lotion for Chest Hair Enhancement" (NCT02283645), was registered with 64 participants and a January 2015 start; its registry status is listed as unknown.[1] No results from it have been published in the sources checked.
infobox: Scalp pattern hair loss (US, topical, OTC since 1996)

paras: Minoxidil was developed by Upjohn and introduced as a blood pressure drug in 1971, when hair growth was noticed as an effect. Topical minoxidil was approved in the US for male hair loss in 1988, for women in 1991, and became over-the-counter in 1996. Topical versions come as 2% or 5% solutions and as a 5% foam or spray.

Minoxidil is sulfated by SULT1A1 to minoxidil sulfate, an ATP-sensitive potassium channel opener. Its action on follicles is not fully understood; suggested contributions include vasodilation, VEGF and other growth factors, and prolongation of the anagen phase.

For topical use, reference sources list itching, scalp irritation, dandruff, temporary shedding and unwanted hair growth elsewhere on the body. Alcohol and propylene glycol in some products can dry skin and cause contact dermatitis. Oral minoxidil is associated with fluid retention, rapid heartbeat, dizziness and hypertrichosis, and rarely pericardial effusion.

Wikipedia reports that hair growth from minoxidil stops once treatment ends: after long-term use is stopped, hair is lost quickly and by about 24 weeks density is similar to that of people given placebo. For scalp hair loss, benefits appear after 2 to 4 months and peak around 12 months.

One registered trial, NCT02283645, was designed to test 3% minoxidil lotion for chest hair enhancement (phase 4, n=64, start date January 2015, status unknown).[1] No published results were found. Studies of minoxidil in scalp hair loss are far more extensive, and studies in beard hair are cited by Wikipedia without results.

lore.intro: Chest hair threads mention topical minoxidil as an option for sparse chests. Accounts are anecdotal.

claims.claim: Topical minoxidil on the chest thickens chest hair.
